lesson.title: What Makes Honey Slow and Water Quick
lesson.summary: Viscosity is a liquid's resistance to flow, and it increases with stronger intermolecular forces and with molecular shapes that let molecules tangle or hold onto each other, which is why honey pours far more slowly than water.
lesson.body:
Viscosity is a measure of a liquid's resistance to flow, or equivalently, its internal friction as layers of the liquid slide past one another. A liquid with high viscosity, like honey or motor oil, flows sluggishly and pours slowly, while a liquid with low viscosity, like water or rubbing alcohol, flows readily and pours quickly. At the particle level, flowing requires molecules to slip past their neighbors continuously, so anything that makes molecules more reluctant to let go of each other increases how much resistance the liquid offers to that slipping motion.

The dominant factor behind viscosity is the same one behind surface tension and boiling point: the strength of the intermolecular forces holding the liquid's molecules to one another. Stronger intermolecular forces mean molecules cling to their neighbors more persistently, so more energy is required to pull one molecule away from its neighbors long enough for it to slide into a new position, which shows up macroscopically as higher viscosity. Water, with its extensive hydrogen bonding network, is noticeably more viscous than pentane, a nonpolar liquid held together only by weaker dispersion forces, even though pentane's molecules are individually much larger and heavier than water's; pentane still pours more freely, which is a clear sign that force type is winning out over molecular size in this comparison.

Molecular shape and size add a second, independent factor on top of intermolecular force strength. Long, chain-like molecules can physically tangle with one another in addition to attracting each other through intermolecular forces, similarly to how a pile of tangled string resists being pulled apart even if the individual strings are not sticky. This is why glycerol, a small molecule with three hydroxyl (O-H) groups capable of extensive hydrogen bonding across a flexible carbon chain, is dramatically more viscous than water at room temperature, and why long-chain hydrocarbons in motor oil are far more viscous than short-chain hydrocarbons in gasoline, even though both are held together by nothing stronger than dispersion forces. The longer chains have more surface area for dispersion forces to act along, and they can also mechanically interfere with each other's motion as they try to slide past one another.

Temperature has a strong and predictable effect on viscosity as well, and it follows directly from the same kinetic energy versus intermolecular force competition used throughout this unit. Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules, giving them more energy to overcome the intermolecular forces or tangling holding them back, which is why honey pours noticeably faster when warmed and why motor oil is formulated differently for cold versus warm climates. Viscosity, surface tension, and boiling point all trace back to the same underlying cause, the strength of the forces between a liquid's molecules, which is exactly why a liquid that scores high on one of these three properties, like water compared to a nonpolar liquid of similar size, tends to score high on the other two as well.
